entries.title: GitHub Ditches CSS-in-JS for CSS Modules, Reports 55% Faster SSR After Three-Year Migration
entries.summary: GitHub migrated github.com from styled-components to CSS Modules over three years, reporting a 55% cut in server-side rendering time and 25% faster component initialisation. Primer components were converted behind feature flags, and about 7,760 sx prop usages were migrated with codemods and Copilot agents. Commenters questioned user impact and hashed class names. By Daniel Curtis
entries.content:
GitHub has published an in-depth account of a three-year effort to move github.com off CSS-in-JS and onto CSS Modules, reporting a 55% reduction in server-side rendering time and 25% faster component initialisation across its Primer-powered design system.

Written by Primer engineers Josh Black and Marie Lucca, the post explains how component counts on certain pages began to explode in 2023, exposing scaling problems with the existing styled-components setup. Initial page loads, server render times and style update costs all grew with component count. The team picked CSS Modules because it kept native CSS features and co-location while removing client and server runtime work, letting styles roll up into static stylesheets delivered with the HTML.

For every Primer component the team added a CSS Modules variant, gated it behind a feature flag, verified parity with visual regression tests, then rolled it out from the Primer team to GitHub staff and finally all users. By December 2024, Primer itself was fully on CSS Modules. The harder half was the roughly 7,760 

sx
prop usages scattered across github.com, the de facto styling standard for years. A transitional 
@primer/styled-react
 package let 
sx
keep working against migrated components during the crossover.

A typical conversion looks like this:

// Before
import { Button } from '@primer/styled-react';


// After
import { Button } from '@primer/react';
import styles from './PayButton.module.css';

A rotation of eight engineers migrated 6,419 props over six months, seeing SSR improvements ranging from 3% up to 22% per page. The final 895 props were cleared in three weeks by two engineers leaning heavily on Copilot coding agents. GitHub also had to decouple theming for its seven themes and high-contrast variants before pulling styled-components out entirely. A VS Code plugin and internal codemod cut the manual burden, and GitHub notes that styled-components entering maintenance mode reinforced the direction.

On Hacker News one commenter running a similar migration reported a 30% build time speed improvement and much better tree shaking on Next.js across a codebase over 1M lines. Others were sceptical about user impact, with one arguing that the reduction in size was not big enough to justify making all CSS names unreadable, adding that hashed class names make ad-blockers, custom CSS and browser extensions harder to build. A separate thread noted that CSS-in-JS can be made zero-runtime without moving to Modules at all.

GitHub joins a broader shift away from runtime CSS-in-JS. Linear recently completed its own 1,000-PR move from styled-components to Meta's atomic StyleX library, citing similar render-time concerns after upgrading to React 18's concurrent mode. Others using vanilla-extract or Tailwind have shifted style generation to build time entirely. The common thread is to pay the cost once at build, not on every request.

The Primer Design System is GitHub's open-source component library, providing the foundational building blocks used across github.com. Teams following the same path can start from the Primer React v38 release notes and the migration guide for CSS variables, which covers the move from sx props to CSS Modules.

entries.title: DoorDash Scales Dispatch 10x While Maintaining 99.99% Peak Availability
entries.summary: DoorDash has redesigned its real-time dispatch platform, replacing a monolithic optimization engine with a distributed architecture that separates coordination from computation. The new system delivers 10x higher throughput and more than 99.99% peak availability. It also supports hybrid machine learning inference and multi-agent reinforcement learning to dynamically optimize delivery assignments.
entries.content:
DoorDash has rebuilt its real-time dispatch platform to handle growing delivery demand, replacing a monolithic optimization engine with a distributed architecture that separates coordination from computation. The redesign delivers 10 times higher throughput and more than 99.99% availability during peak periods, while enabling the company to run machine learning and reinforcement learning models within dispatch workflows.

The previous dispatch engine tightly coupled business logic, logistics state management, and computationally intensive routing algorithms. As delivery volume increased, its optimization workload became increasingly difficult to process within the time available for dispatch decisions. The underlying algorithms had roughly quadratic time complexity, and during peak periods, demand approached four times the system's processing capacity. The engine consequently relied on fallback heuristics and sometimes made assignment decisions using incomplete information.

As the DoorDash engineering team explained:

The fatal bottleneck wasn't just raw machine capacity; it was the speed of reality.

Rather than address the bottleneck through conventional horizontal scaling, DoorDash redesigned the execution model around two independently scalable tiers. The engineering team described the motivation:

To scale into the future, the system didn't just need more capacity; it demanded a fundamentally new execution model.

The new platform separates execution into two independently scalable tiers. A stateful coordinator manages dispatch lifecycles, maintains global logistics state, and validates business rules. Stateless compute workers handle mathematical optimization, vehicle-routing heuristics, and model inference.

The coordinator distributes localized portions of logistics data to workers using payload sharding over gRPC. This avoids broadcasting the entire global state to every worker and reduces network overhead. Workers process their assigned optimization tasks independently, while the coordinator manages orchestration and result aggregation.

Evolution from DoorDash's monolithic dispatch engine to its distributed architecture (Source: DoorDash Blog Post)

The redesign addresses computational complexity through hierarchical decomposition. Rather than solving one global optimization problem, the coordinator partitions logistics data into geographic clusters and delivery trajectories. Workers process smaller problems in parallel, and a reconciliation layer combines results across partitions.

DoorDash used shadow testing before directing live dispatch decisions to the new platform. Production requests were duplicated, with the legacy engine determining assignments while the new platform's outputs were logged for comparison. Teams evaluated matching quality, delivery times, and resilience under load. After establishing parity, they used controlled switchback experiments and fallback mechanisms during rollout.

Shadow testing compares legacy and new dispatch outputs (Source: DoorDash Blog Post)

DoorDash reports a tenfold increase in dispatch throughput, with more than 99.96% of runs completing within 20 seconds. During Super Bowl Sunday, the platform maintained more than 99.99% availability despite a 10% week-over-week increase in peak volume.

The architecture also introduces a hybrid L1/L2 model serving. Latency-sensitive inference runs locally within compute workers using ONNX Runtime, avoiding remote procedure call overhead. More complex evaluations use isolated remote model-serving clusters, keeping heavier workloads away from the coordinator's state-management path.

DoorDash has also deployed multi-agent reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust dispatch objective weights based on localized marketplace feedback, including merchant congestion and courier utilization. The agents adapt the trade-off between delivery speed and batching efficiency at individual stores. The approach was evaluated through production switchback experiments and accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Reinforcement Learning from World Feedback.

entries.title: Vercel Launched Experimental Board to Coordinate Tasks Across Humans and Coding Agents
entries.summary: Vercel's experimental Board is a headless message store where people and coding agents claim leased tasks, declare dependencies, and sync threads with Slack, GitHub, and Linear. By Daniel Dominguez
entries.content:
Vercel has launched Vercel Board, an experimental, headless message board where people and coding agents coordinate tasks across tools and harnesses. Vercel says Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, eve, fx, Mastra, and LangChain can work on the same board as if they were a single harness.

Each Vercel team gets a default board, named General, organized into channels and threads. Developers and agents read and write through the `vercel board` CLI or the `@vercel/board` JavaScript SDK. A skill, installed with 

npx skills add vercel/board --skill board
, teaches coding agents the CLI. Agents name themselves with 
--as
or 
BOARD_PROFILE
, but still act with the operator's or project's credentials.

A task is a thread whose state the board keeps. A worker claims a ready task, posts updates, and completes or fails it. A claim is a lease of up to five minutes and must be renewed; if it expires, the task returns to the queue. When two workers claim the same task, one succeeds and the other fails with 

task_claimed
. Tasks can declare dependencies, so a review waits until its fix completes while independent work proceeds in parallel. Watchers on a Vercel deployment can run when a reply is posted or a label changes, waking the deployment so no process has to stay running.

Sync, configured in the SDK and delivered through Vercel Connect, can attach a board channel to Slack, GitHub, or Linear. Slack and Linear sync both ways; GitHub imports pull requests and issues and does not write back unless the project sends those messages. Grants control who can read, post, and manage each channel. For an agent in a Vercel Sandbox, 

sandboxPolicy()
can grant limited board access without putting a credential inside the sandbox. Vercel says it rebuilt v0's software factory on Board, and that the factory now merges over 50% of its pull requests.

Official documentation warns that Board grants do not apply on Slack, GitHub, or Linear, so a private Slack channel synced into an open board channel is readable by the whole Vercel team.

Austin King (@MadeWithOzten) replied to Vercel's announcement asking to 

Do this self-hosted and open source - Rust, Yjs Sync,

then wrote that he had bought openboard.lol 

For a self-hosted open source Vercel board like thing.

Aaron Delz (@AaronDelz) said he already kept a shared checklist with his agent, and liked that a Board task can be completed with the pull request attached:

Same rule my agents run on: no saying 'done' without the evidence.

Similar coordination shows up elsewhere. OpenCrawl is an open source, self-hostable board that also records agent sessions. GitHub Agent HQ can assign issues and pull requests to Copilot, Claude, or Codex. Linear's cloud coding agent turns scoped issues into draft pull requests with Claude Code or Codex. Claude Code agent teams coordinate multiple Claude Code sessions around a shared task list, and the Agent2Agent protocol standardizes delegation between agents rather than hosting a board.

Board remains experimental infrastructure on a Vercel team. Setup steps and the CLI and SDK references are in Vercel's Board documentation

entries.title: Presentation: Learning Out Loud (Under Near-Existential Pressure)
entries.summary: Laura Savino discusses the psychological friction of AI adoption for senior engineers & architects. She explains how shifting from static expertise to learning in public lowers anxiety, accelerates tooling fluency, and prevents burnout. Leaders will discover actionable strategies to support their teams, debunk tech zealotry, and foster an adaptive engineering culture that thrives during upheaval.
entries.content:
Transcript

Laura Savino: Several friends and colleagues have come to me to tell me recently that they are pregnant with their first child, and have taken comfort from a really odd bit of perspective that I've given them, because I have two lovely kids, two very much wanted and uneventful pregnancies. I hated being pregnant. Every so often, I look around a crowd of people, and I'm like, everyone here is the result of a pregnancy, and it creeps me out. It's beautiful. It's a miracle of life. It is also not my jam. The thing that made me willing to do it at all and that gave me great comfort along the way was actually the myth of the frog. This frog is swimming around in water that starts at a comfortable temperature, but is slowly heated through to a boil, and if you do it gradually enough, the frog won't really notice that its environment is no longer like anything it's ever experienced before, and the frog is eventually cooked.

This odd myth gave me a lifeline of hope, because if that frog can adapt to extreme, unprecedented conditions, so can I. Because the difficult parts usually come on gradually, day by day. If having a child started with the eighth-month pregnancy discomfort, very few of us would do it. It would be banned as inhumane torture if we could instantly make people eight months pregnant.

Some of you are like, "It's 9:00 in the morning. We're at a software conference. Can we please not talk about spontaneous advanced gestation? It is a repulsive idea." When we see a person eight months pregnant who got there gradually, the way we all luckily do, we just think, how nice. It's not repulsive at all, it's beautiful. It's usually obvious that they're just handling it like champions. It turns out the frog thing is thoroughly debunked. At a certain point, ectotherms change locations to keep themselves safe. The myth works to reassure me and my pregnant friends because of the way I frame it. It's not that the thing gets worse and worse slowly, and you don't notice and eventually are cooked. It's that you yourself change. You adapt. Yes, your context becomes more and more difficult, but if you're committed to sticking it out, you flex some increasingly creative coping strategies and skills, you become able to handle it. You worry about eighth month after you've figured out the seventh month and the sixth month, you'll be fine.

Let's tangent from there. I have these two amazing kids, one is 8. We've had Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse on repeat in our house this past month. There's this one scene that captures me. A newly bitten Spider-Man is trying to learn to thwip, that's the technical term, and he's doing it while being chased by an evil giant robo-scientist through the trees, so Spider-Man is like dodging trees, and he yells, "Whoa, whoa, I can't do this yet." His trainer quips, "Everyone knows that the best way to learn is under intense, life-threatening pressure." Another anecdote. My friend TJ. TJ is an all-around delightful person, but their rarest trait and the highest compliment that I can reach for is that they are a functional programming language aficionado and are not an asshole about it. These days we're all a little or a lot more on board with the functional aspects of Rust and Kotlin and Swift, and strongly preferring pure functions is just mainstream now.

Side Effect punk is dead. Remember Haskell, the language? Remember when there was a whole functional programming dogma with true believers, with the hyper-conviction of the newly converted, and there were memes about monads. If your brain could follow certain logical compressions, you were with it. You were good. You were likely to survive, and everybody else was getting left in the imperative rubble. When I learned TJ appreciated Haskell, I was like, but you're so chill about it. They were like, it's a really interesting tool. This was the first time that I'd met a functional programming enthusiast that I could relate to.

Background

I am Laura Savino. I'm a developer on Photoshop, somewhat on the iOS UI, but also on the C++ library that supports real Photoshop PSD file editing on your phone. Before I became a software engineer, I thought I was going to be a language teacher. I was for a minute. I took master's-level courses in things like how to teach American English pronunciation, how to design a test that tests what you want it to evaluate, which is hard. I taught English in France and French in Seattle, and English again at that time in South Korea, and eventually learned to code. Fast-forward several years, and here I am on the QCon London stage. Today's talk, I hope, will start to shift your identity from someone who's good at doing a specific thing to someone who's good at learning near anything. I'm taking it as an anthology of vignettes with research for structural support. In rough order of appearance, so you have a sense of time passing. There will be cabinet-making, teen vampires, December-born horses, a Zen priest, football kits, awkward dance floors, and a puppy. I will provide a slide with references at the end, so you can settle in.

The Onslaught of AI

I started with three stories, one about a frog, one about Spider-Man, and one about these monad pushers, and this is not exactly an un-telegraphed reveal that these stories map shockingly neatly onto the onslaught of AI. The first one, the frog metaphor that comforted me so much in my pregnancy, part of what makes the AI transition so disorienting is that we're being asked, many of us, to take it on. Like, now, now, now, the water is plasma, and you frogs will get in there, and you will like it. If you're not already orchestrating, you're so far behind, you might as well take up goat herding, because the goats are more your speed. For Spider-Man, a big reason the AI transition is so daunting is that many people's livelihoods are directly tied to how well we adapt. It's fine. The robot arm's chasing us, they're motivating. We all just ducked in here for a minute to throw them off our trails.

Lastly, about my chill friend, it's tough out there because of all the zealots. I think most of them are not actually assholes. I genuinely believe they're mostly just excited, and they cannot imagine a reasonable person in possession of all the facts who's not exactly as excited as they are. They respond by either assuming you're an unreasonable person or giving you more facts, and I'm not sure which is worse. The ultimate well-meaning zealot is the Chris Traeger character on Parks and Rec played by Rob Lowe. This character is intense, precise, and painfully optimistic. There's this one scene where he says he's logged 65,000 miles running in his lifetime, and his goal is to run to the moon. Some AI enthusiasts are giving a little Chris Traeger running to the moon. We recognize they're telling us about something healthy and good, and they may even have our best interests at heart, but no part of me wishes I had my running shoes on so I could join him to the moon. How do we bring people with us?

On the Bleeding Edge

I experienced a massive at-the-time transition in Cocoa, in the Apple development community that did this well. See, it was possible for a long time to go into Apple development with a great deal of hubris. You were an Apple developer. You knew all the tricks and tips. You'd hand-molded a lock and knit release cycles. Back of the cabinet here means, sure, no one's going to see this part of the code, but we're still going to make it just so because we take pride in our work. For a minute there, you could be confident that your deep UI kit and Objective-C knowledge meant that big companies would pay you and a team of three or four devs and a crack designer, absolute truckloads of cash to write them an app because everyone needed apps and no one knew how to write them except us. It was a really good time to be an Apple developer.

Then Apple dropped Swift, brand new language. You're welcome, everyone. Soon all our new APIs will be in this brand-new language that you have to use. We were willing to give up our semicolons. No one likes those, but they ripped away our square brackets too. This was one of those watershed community moments. One perspective I really liked at the time was, we're knocked back to being beginners again, and we like it. We're on even footing. We're learning together. Isn't this exciting? The change electrified us in good and bad ways. On the good side, I distinctly remember watching people who'd shipped indie software on CDs, people who were intimately familiar with why NSString is prefixed that way because they used to code in NEXTSTEP. These developers dived headfirst into the new language. I was sitting around with The Omni Group folks, like OmniFocus, OmniGraffle, these are Apple ecosystem legends, with our laptops out in the hotel lobbies of San Francisco, just trying to figure out, what can I do with this new language? On the less good side.

Swift was announced in June, and on my production app, we had an intern who waited several weeks till late July, before Xcode, our IDE was even out of beta, the intern added Swift to the project just for fun. The tool chain support was abysmal. I couldn't exactly embrace the beginner's mind when I was trying to ship a feature and couldn't even type because my IDE kept lagging out with this message. It was frustrating and not at all production ready because the tool chain was literally in beta. On the whole, with the benefit of rose-colored nostalgia, it was good. Most super senior principal developers, these pinnacles of technical excellence, were having to relearn how to get the eighth element out of a string, like just rookie stuff. The behaviors that got rewarded were the ones where people learned in public. The people who learned the most were the ones who asked the most questions, who'd notice when they didn't understand something and say, this is something I don't understand.

How interesting? They'd post forum questions and ask each other how things worked. They would post early code samples where they did not look like geniuses who knew all the answers, but just enthusiastic rookies who wanted to learn. You know how much people love correcting people on the internet, so anyone who posted something inaccurate got told about it real quick. How do you be ok with that, though? How do you psychologically handle going from the expert hot commodity to a total noob and keep up decent spirits while you do it?

First and Second Order Denial

My friends, has anyone considered the old standby straight-up denial? I don't think any of us are in first-order denial about AI where we refuse to accept that it exists or is changing things, but for myself, I am absolutely deep in second-order denial where you acknowledge the basic facts of the thing, but you deny the implications of those facts. Sure, the technology is here, but I am not ready to face its implications. I usually try to add a lot of details when I'm giving a talk, but here, I am going to kindly draw a veil and let the camera discreetly pan away because you do not need me to share my particular doomsday flavors. Besides, it weakens the denial. Denial can also stem from a fear that you or those you love lack the skills or resources to handle the consequences of a change. That's real.

Apparently, denial can have protective effects, though. This one study, "The role of denial in recovery from coronary heart disease," found that people who were in deep denial actually had better short-term outcomes than the ones who were actually facing reality. If you had deeper denial, you'd spend less time in intensive care and have fewer heart-related symptoms while you were in hospital. This rings true for me. Even if I've decided a thing is important to me, even when it's well-aligned with my values, if I face the full implications of how hard it's going to be, I will probably not do it. I might say, I don't have to exercise at the gym. I'm just going to put my shoes on and show up and we'll just see what happens. Denial can work to get us to start down a hard road and give us hope long enough to adapt to this ever-changing water.

Protective denial, it's incredibly common. We're also all going to die someday, but memento mori has somehow fallen out of fashion. If you want to sit in second-order denial with me for a little longer, that's ok. For a little longer, because the heart patients with serious denial had worse outcomes long-term. They didn't follow their medical advice, because why would they? They were fine. They got re-hospitalized more. Denial is not sustainable. If a little self-misdirection is what it takes to follow your values to stay in the room and not make a down payment on a yacht, go ahead, indulge. Let me suggest another indulgence, brain candy. When I was trying to improve my Spanish, I read the Twilight books, and I'm guessing most of you haven't read them or won't admit to having read them, because they're cloying vampire, werewolf, romance novels written for pre-teens. My Spanish became tan brillante como el pelo de Eduardo a la luz del sol, because brain candy, in the domain you're trying to learn, is just like the little carrot thrown down the path to convince the recalcitrant, what, I'm supposed to be good at this part of you, to at least look over and start to think about how to maybe head down this otherwise daunting path.

Sometimes you truly need to lower the stakes mentally just so you can push through. Get out of that intense, life-threatening pressure. Solve an actual problem that only you have. Make some tool, make some toy, make a flatulence app with your 8-year-old, something real, but where no one will evaluate you on the outcome because evaluation changes us. We don't learn so we can achieve the task we care about, we learn to pass the test assigned to us. This is bad even if you're an excellent test taker.

Building Fluency

I took a break from my French major one summer to spend eight weeks in an intensive Japanese language study in northern Japan, where they promised to teach us the equivalent of two university semesters of Japanese. I was very good at French at that point. I had just breezed through a pair of graduate seminars and my placement test in the Japanese program put me in the very lowest level class. I'd only taken two basic Japanese classes by this point, but I just still felt like, "Hello, don't you know who I am? I'm good at languages. Why am I in the beginner's class with these people who can barely put a sentence together?" Granted, I couldn't say, do you know who I am, in Japanese, which is maybe a sign that their class placement was somewhat valid, but I had a demonstrated skill in a fundamentally different but still related area.

Some of us are feeling this way about computing right now. I'm good at computers. I am a senior professional programmer. I once learned Python in an afternoon. If this new computing skill is hard for me, either is something is wrong with the system or something is wrong with me. Don't you know who I am? For me in Japan, my identity was so caught up in being good at languages that I worked hard to avoid ever making a mistake, not just on coursework, but asking the bus driver for a transfer ticket. I wanted my Japanese to be perfect. I actually learned the most about learning that summer on a weekend excursion, just me and a classmate, where we stayed at a family-run Buddhist temple out in the countryside. I won't go into the expectation thrashing experience of preparing myself for a solemn weekend of meditation and instead watching sumo wrestling on TV with a priest and his family, but the larger foundation-shattering surprise was the way my classmate spoke to our Japanese hosts and that she would just say things.

She'd trip over words. She'd mess up her verb endings. My grammar wasn't great, but I could recognize a bunch of mistakes even if I couldn't correct them. I was so deep in this prove to everyone that I'm good at this mentality that if I didn't know how to say something properly, I'd keep quiet so I didn't embarrass myself. Amy, though, just talked. They're like laughing, conversing. The priest gets another beer. What stuck with me long after I forgot all the extra kanji I learned that summer, is that interacting imperfectly builds fluency. You get early feedback before unwanted behaviors are calcified. Find your version of a Zen retreat where you can just play with the tools with no expectations of evaluation. You'll develop facility and fluency that much faster.

Another way to fail when something's not a test. Many years ago, as I was just learning to code, like mapping out how to do red-black trees on a whiteboard level, I went out with some friends and some friends of friends to rent a karaoke room. One of these friends of friends turned out to be an engineering manager at Microsoft, which is a hazard of where I live in Seattle. I remember the fear and dread and shame that I felt when I was unable to successfully navigate the karaoke interface via any of the in-room remote controls. See, I saw this as my chance to prove my technical prowess and maybe get hired on at Microsoft. Why would the engineering manager consider my resume if I couldn't even modify the output settings of a retro karaoke system? I don't remember what any of us saying, but I do remember holding that remote in my hand and thinking that I was never going to get a job in tech.

Now we're all looking back at 15 years ago me and inwardly shouting, everybody knows these systems are hard. Just try, don't give up, it's fine. We have so much compassion. What is your tool today that you're like, I still don't have this thing working. What are they all going to think of me? I better hide it and fake it and just play it cool. If you have that mental block, lower the stakes, make a tool, make a toy, something unspeakably inane that is tailored to exactly your interests. It can lower the activation energy required to take that next step towards learning.

Another way I make daunting things feel more approachable is thinking of them as a practice round. Picture this, every Sunday morning, I'm at a former aircraft hangar that's been turned into an indoor kids' sports hell hole arena. There are five football fields, a dozen simultaneous kid classes, there's adult workout classes, there's birthday rooms, plus an enormous bouncy house situation. I promise you whatever you're picturing, there are more bouncy houses. There's screaming and there's tears and there's kids running and begging for snacks, and I'm paying to be here. I went to great effort to dig the 4-year-old's soccer uniform out of his dirty laundry hamper and convince him to leave the house and convince him to leave the car. My reward for that is sitting on an uncomfortable bench drinking truly some of the worst coffee in Seattle. I want to paint for you this picture of aggressively, brightly colored despair, because what you need to appreciate is that it was a big deal for me to change perspectives.

Because I realize that if you see this not as a whole collection of circumstances designed to maximize my suffering, but hundreds of families who each separately fought through the chaos that is having a child on a chilly, damp weekend morning and got them to leave the house. If we could see in a little heads-up display what people overcame to get through that door, we would be walking around high-fiving and pouring each other pints. Nobody mentions all these hurdles. They just act like, yes, kids are wearing their kits here on time, relatively few boogers, as if they didn't execute a dozen fancy maneuvers to get there. If I don't tell someone that I struggled to get my kid there dressed, I won't hear their advice. Yes, my kid sleeps in her football kit. Sunday mornings have become my time to bask in the glory that not only have all of us made it through a gauntlet, but we've also successfully identified flaws in our own getting-out-of-the-house systems.

We're basically red teaming our own lives. How did you do at getting out of the house without yelling and tears? C-minus. How will you do at learning from what went wrong? Are you committed to bringing better snacks next time? The point isn't how well you executed the thing today, but how well you've internalized and applied the changes for next time. Put the snacks in the car right now, and today counts as a success.

Generating Energy to Learn

When I was deciding whether to take this job I had at Photoshop, I called up a friend for advice, because I had two offers for very different jobs, one that I was sure I would be good at, that they would be lucky to have me, and the other was a stretch. It was on Photoshop, where I'd have to brush up on modern C++ and L1 caches and deal with real legacy code. My friend said that if I had the appetite to learn the new thing, the hard thing, that I should do it now. Because at some point, he said, you're like, I don't want to learn a whole new paradigm again. I've been there. I've done that. I'm good. This advice was perfect when I was choosing my destiny, and learning modern C++ was supposed to be my last big career challenge. Now, very few of us have a choice about whether to invest a ton of energy in learning this new thing.

I have to somehow generate energy for learning or hit burnout real hard. I feel like maybe external energy building works for salespeople. Like I could just shout, are you ready? Let's get pumped. Everyone would be like, yes, let's go. We're engineers who got to where we are by taking skepticism to an art form. How many people have looked at some shiny new tech, said, no, and then just watched it crumble off into the sunset? No amount of like, rah, rah, do it, is going to convince us in all of the do it, learn, go. It's like being told by a scowling Simon Cowell to do a heartfelt interpretive dance. You're not at your best. How do we, the hopeful skeptics who do believe in a better future, in spite of it all, how do we generate energy to learn? Let's actually start by not spiraling, perhaps, by not leaking happiness.

One way I patch the leak is comparing current me to past me, because I'm obviously better than I was 10 years ago, aren't you? Think of you 10 years ago, and the glimmers of what you most value now that we're just starting to show. We were all goobers then compared to us now. Yet, we are all deeply discounting how much wiser we will be in the next 10 years, because we've got it figured out now. This is an actual studied phenomenon with a whole name, the end of history illusion. More specifically, we see the present as the moment where we have finally become the person we'll be for the rest of our lives.

More published sources. Just this year, Dr. Maya Shankar published a really timely book called "The Other Side of Change." I feel like she gets us as software people today, because she was well on the path to becoming a professional violinist when she had a career-ending injury, at which point she went into the field of psychology. She eventually became the behavioral sciences advisor to the UN. She did all right. I am clinging to her perspectives like a lifeline. She adds to this end of history idea, not about years, but any large change, when we imagine what it will be like to navigate an unexpected change and its aftermath, we tend to assume that we'll be the same person from beginning to end. Research shows that we greatly underestimate how much we'll change in the future, even though we fully acknowledge that we've changed considerably in the past.

Am I just going to keep reading you quotes? Yes, I am. Because these are literally professional studiers of brains, and they said this better than I can. You can think of this as the audiobook interlude. "The unique stresses and demands of being thrust into a new reality can uncover unexpected insights about ourselves and the world around us. These insights, coupled with the experience of the change itself, can transform us in extraordinary ways." I hear that, and I externally nod. Like, yes, maybe I'll grow on the other side of whatever this unprecedented time is. Also, a small part of me throws an absolute foot-stomping fit. I do not want to. I've barely got it together with the current state of things, and now you're coming at me with, think of all the personal growth you'll get. Like, no, I'm sorry. How many people are actively fantasizing about goat-herding careers right now?

There is some comfort in knowing that the person who will undergo the full experience will be different from the person we are in this very moment. We will become new people on the other side of change in ways we are capable of shaping. I still don't want to. I don't. I remind myself to take a breath, or six, because, see, the frog is facing physical challenges and doesn't have biohacking tools there in its pot. Our challenges are all in our minds, for better or worse. As my favorite book series says, my head is where 90-plus percent of my problems are. We believe in neuroplasticity. We can change and grow our minds from the inside out. I promise this is related, but did you know in the competitive equine sports world, all horses have the same official birthday? In the Northern Hemisphere, they all turn one year older on January 1st.

That means that if your horse was born on New Year's Eve, for juvenile racing purposes, they'll be considered 2 years old when they turn 366 days. You can see how a 700-day-old 2-year-old race horse would have an advantage. Breeders often arrange for foals to be born as close to January 2nd as they can. Football in the States has the same effect, actually, where a statistically improbable number of professional footballers are born in the first quartile of the year. Few parents plan their kids' births around the football season for some reason. There's something to be said for always being a little ahead of your peer group. You literally win more. If the kids on your football team look up to you because they're barely 6 while you're nearly 7, and coaches look to you to lead the team's comeback when they're behind 3-0, you develop leadership skills and confidence from a very early age.

I am on the other side. I came to technology late, so I got used to seeking coding advice from literal teenagers from day one of my first professional programming job. Since then, every team I'm on, I've been in the middle quartile in terms of raw technical Leet code acumen. Before anyone starts DMing me about imposter syndrome and telling me to believe in myself, I'm going to stop you, because I'm on the Photoshop engineering team, and I'm solidly in the middle of the pack. It's like being in the bottom third of Man City players, like, I'm one of the worst world-class athletes. Like, it's fine. I'm no slouch. I just keep moving up to better and better leagues. Because I started out behind and have stayed in the middle, I've never developed an ego around being the fastest prototyper or the most effective algorithm tuner. I have learned how to learn.

The Growth Mindset, and Learning in Public

There's this famous study on which learning tasks people will take if given the option to improve their skills. One task is advertised as majorly effective, the other as so-so. It turns out the researchers could easily influence which participants chose which task. See, in the ineffective task, people could try and fail privately, and the highly effective one involved practicing in front of the group so everyone saw your mistakes. Clearly different paths with different risks and outcomes, and you all might have a sense of which group you would tend towards. How would a researcher influence you to pick one over the other? They gave people reading material about the malleability of the particular skill, debating in this case. One group read that debate is mostly an innate skill, the other that anyone can do it. It just takes training. It takes practice. The people who were in the inborn skill group, they did not participate in the activity that would help them improve, because then everybody would see that they lacked the skill.

The trainable skill group people were like, ok, let's go. Who cares if other people see that I can't do this yet? Showing people you're ignorant of something today can and should be super low stakes. It goes along with believing in neuroplasticity. This study is out of Carol Dweck's research about growth mindset, which had a whole Silicon Valley trend moment. I think it's not as trendy now, but the research is still solid. People who believe that their traits and abilities can significantly change are more likely to engage in behaviors that improve them. One problem that I ran into face first, like a very clean plate glass door one, is that when you start paying attention to whether you have a growth mindset and realize that without the researcher's priming that you would definitely be in the group that's like, better make sure no one finds out I'm a terrible debater.

It throws you extra, because you, by definition, don't really believe that you can change how fixed your mindset is. These research scientists, I have to believe them because they approach this problem with rigor and with science at Stanford. They say quite plainly that cherished traits can be developed. I want to be better at believing in change and in neuroplasticity, so I'm working on it.

Part of my identity has become someone who learns out loud, and I've modeled learning out loud in public. The first time a principal engineer on the Photoshop team wanted to show me how to use a new AI tool to bolt a tricky feature onto our existing architecture, I recorded our screen share session and posted it for the rest of the team because seeing a tool used in a real-world context is always more instructive than the demo-worthy vacuum. Especially because, like all my comrades who brought their kids to weekend morning soccer practices, we each come to AI and use AI in completely different ways. My favorite take on this is from Dr. Cat Hicks. She is a research psychologist studying software teams and gets riled up in a very data-driven way when people talk about things like measuring team effectiveness. She emphasizes that none of us are having the same experience.

"When you have a highly adaptive, dialogical tool," which means the user is in dialogue with the tool, "where the user is shaping the context and wielding progressive disclosure to probe very different parts of its capabilities, different people will continue to get very different answers. Until we get real about the personalized, adaptive nature of this." People are each running their own individual experiments with new tools, and if we don't tell each other what our own tool uses look like, no one will know that you can put your kid to bed already wearing their football kit. This is not the time to experiment alone until your output seems to resemble other people's. Plus, even if I just complain about a tool, I usually get some really good alternative suggestions. Even though we've all transcended onto this higher plane of mental abstractions, there is still value in showing your actual footwork. Where did your tool fall over? Why did you keep using it anyway?

I actually literally do this in a surprising social context. Otherwise, awkward dance floors. Specifically at weddings or oddly corporate events that have decided to have a dance floor. Basically, collections of people of very mixed abilities who don't know each other super well and yet are celebrating something important together. I pride myself on understanding the assignment to look like I am enjoying myself in a way that invites other people in. I am very specifically not dancing like no one's watching. I am dancing like there's no downside to looking like a goon. I actually want people to see me and think, what a goon? That actually looks fun. Then I, as an enthusiastically mediocre dancer, will also have more fun because more people will be dancing. I also do this in socio-professional groups. I run a biweekly hallway track meeting for Photoshop developers where we just get together and talk off the record about our most recent formal meeting.

Sometimes there's a lull in the conversation. I'll just jump in with an inane comment, sometimes a spicy question, just to let people know we aren't here trying to impress each other. I'll set the bar and then open the door and get out of the way because I love hearing experienced people hash things out. Being mediocre in public can invite people out with you. It brings out other intermediate-level folks. It brings out some shy experts because you've made it obvious that the bar for participation is one that they can easily clear. Now you're in a group of people sharing information and refining ideas before they've fully calcified, and you make each other better. Don't wait to be an expert to join a conversation about your tools. A caveat, when I tell people my advice to be joyfully imperfect in public, I usually mean it a little bit glibly.

Like in the sense of, but obviously not things that are core to your central identity. That would be terrible. No, like I can take up watercolors and show people that I'm an amusingly bad artist, or take up Chinese and let people laugh. When your skill at something is core to your identity, being mediocre in public is like doing a penance for a sin that you didn't even really get to enjoy committing. What I'm trying to do with every fiber of my being is to push this other skill, this meta skill of learning and adapting to change even deeper into my identity and recognizing that this squeaky, uncomfortable like, no, I'm terrible at this. It's like the lactic acid buildup the day after a workout. Is it comfortable? No, it sucks. It is the concrete feeling of getting better.

Bringing People Along

Some of you have been quietly bemused during this whole, here's how to not give up and survive section, because you are fully into learning the new thing. You are like, I am literally a core contributor on Gas Town, my good lady, what are you on about? This next section is for you. See, given the choice, I would rather dance than talk about the weather. I find it less awkward. Sorry, England. If I had absolute power, every awkward silence would just meld seamlessly into a dance break. Yet, I have not once committed the faux pas of grabbing some poor soul by the hand and dragging them onto the dance floor. I would never. Imagine this? You're sitting there at your linen-covered table trying to remember which wine was yours, and some absolute zealot comes and drags you by the hand onto the dance floor and then cheerfully bops away.

You're welcome. It's not ok. Unless you very quickly find your own groove, as soon as you can get away with it, you will moonwalk right back to the table straight past both glasses of wine because this time you're choosing a table much farther from these diehards who keep trying to force you into places where you don't think you fit. People who are happy on the dance floor need to make it more obvious that this is a good place to be and not just keep shouting that all of the non-dance floor is lava and we're getting left behind. Another aspect of bringing people with you. A few months ago, I used an AI agent to help me plan out decluttering my basement. I described the state of years of kid clutter accumulation, and listed off a couple sample starting ideas like disassembling the massive tower of cardboard box sculptures my kid had made, or sorting and condensing the various containers that were half full of miscellaneous.

Cursor came back with a useful plan and some excellent advice, which included, do not start with the miscellaneous bins. They will just exhaust you. Better to focus on low-decision weight, high-impact tasks. You all sighed with relief along there with me. Like, "Low-decision weight, high-impact? Yes, this plan will work. It's going to feel so good and productive." It did. I got the tower out. I got rid of expired food and old toiletries. I made so many easy decisions, and I wrapped up the day feeling tired but satisfied and a good day's work. Then I go to work the next day, and the AI agents are like, "Good, you're back. I saved all these high-decision weight tasks for you. You're welcome." It turns out I'm not the only one who's had this, hold up, I feel like I'm doing more work now. We're working harder. Birgitta mentioned this too.

We are tired. Please keep in mind that when you're telling people how great this tool is, it is not zero cost. It is free as in puppy. You can't just drop it on people's doorsteps. If you're walking around insisting that everyone adopts one, you've got to provide material support. One specific practice, Photoshop's strongest AI tooling advocates host weekly office hours. We're constantly re-explaining to each other how to export the right environment variables this week. The support is critical because you're asking people to work harder. If you're patient when you're asking someone if they've sourced their, Oh My Zsh config recently, they're more likely to keep trying your next, "You'll like this one, I promise." They're more likely to try that idea.

Fear of Lack of Skills

I know that some of you are very worried that some of us aren't fully embracing how different our jobs will be in five years. I actually said that to troll you a little because I know it's an order of magnitude faster. Remember that a source of denial can be a lack of certainty that we have the skills to deal with the change. The more you remind your teams and your colleagues that they have done hard things before, that they can learn and grow, that neuroplasticity is real, the more they can loosen their hold on denial. The more we all believe that we do have the skills to face it, the more likely we are to engage in real protective behaviors. My favorite researcher, Cat Hicks, again, if our teams have a culture of learning, we report more productivity. This next part is me, non-professional scientist, extrapolating, but I think if you have a choice between a team with one expert tool user and a team who believes that they can learn and has faith in the organizational support behind it, choose the team that identifies as learners, the team that thinks they can't use the tool yet.

Why, and How Are We Here?

Why are we here? This is a question whose spiritual pay grade is much higher than mine. I'm going to narrow it to something that I'm actually qualified to speak to, how did we get here? First, approximately one lifetime ago, a lot of people suffered through a lot of months of pregnancy. Some number of years ago, we went from not knowing technology to being paid to be good at it. Some number of weeks ago, we all decided it was a good use of three solid days of our time to sit at a tech conference, and then every single person got it together and left their home. If we had heads-up displays showing each of our logistical contortions we used to get here, we would be high-fiving and pouring each other pints all day. We all decided that, yes, it's worth it to take that skeptically optimistic next step to learn a new thing from a stranger rather than chatting up friends in the hall.

We've been through a lot to get here, and it's all been in the mad hope of finding that next good thing. We got here, and here and now is oddly harder than anything our industry has encountered, and even this is just a practice round for the next. The beginner's mindset that you're dusting off, the resilience that you did not want to have to shore up, and the communities that you're building now, this is not the last time you'll be calling on them. We're all just brains in training for the next swell, so if you usually avoid things that make you feel like a December-born horse, take a minute to practice being new at things. Start with watercolors if you want, but also today you could go to a talk whose topic intimidates you. If a popular or mandated tool is giving you blisters, you can say so.

Talk to your peers to commiserate, to your juniors so they know it's not just them, to your management if you've got some political capital burning a hole in your Slack drafts. This is what leadership looks like in this world where everyone's a beginner. It looks like being unafraid to say, don't you know who I am? Yes, I'm someone who learns out loud.

entries.title: Rust 1.100 Ships the Never Type After Ten Years and Five Failed Attempts
entries.summary: Rust 1.100.0, released 12 November 2026, stabilises the never type (!) after ten years of work and makes Infallible an alias for it. The release also stabilises the core of the allocator API, adds DropGuard, and gives Cargo an opt-in dependency cooldown setting. Some critics note the allocator design still lacks inline storage support. By Daniel Curtis
entries.content:
The Rust team has released Rust 1.100.0, the language's first three-digit stable version, with a release that finally lands the never type after a decade of work. Announced on 12 November 2026, the release also stabilises the core of the custom allocator API, introduces a 

DropGuard
helper, and gives Cargo opt-in dependency cooldowns and warnings for unused dependencies.

The headline is the stabilisation of 

!
, the canonical uninhabited type for computations that never return a value, such as 
panic!()
, 
return
or an endless loop. Although functions have long used it as a return type, naming it elsewhere, for instance writing 
Result
to describe an operation that cannot fail, took ten years and five failed stabilisation attempts to land. The release also makes 
std::convert::Infallible
an alias for 
!
, which is what the type was always intended to be, so existing APIs using 
Infallible
now accept 
!
transparently.

To make that alias work, the team shipped a small breaking change for the 2015, 2018 and 2021 editions, flipping the never-type fallback from 

()
to 
!
and matching behaviour already introduced in Rust 2024. The release notes describe the impact as largely unnoticeable but warn that more code may be flagged as unreachable. Developers hitting issues on upgrade are advised to update dependencies first, since fixes for widely used crates have already been published.

The core of the long-awaited 

allocator_api
is also now stable, letting library authors define custom allocators used with 
Vec
and 
Box
through the new 
Allocator
trait. This forms the foundation of the Allocators 1.0 project goal. Critics on the internals forum have argued that Rust still lacks Zig's granular control over allocation because the current design cannot support inline storage, with moves invalidating internal pointers, but the stabilised core is seen as a workable starting point for broader collections support.

On the Hacker News release post, one user noted that some of the changes weren’t mentioned in the blog post for the release:

This release is so big that multiple useful stabilized API aren't event mentioned in the blog post like:

  • bool::toggle() https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/primitive.bool.html#met...
  • Box::map() https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/boxed/struct.Box.html#m...
  • str::trim_prefix(), str::trim_suffix, Path::trim_prefix()

The new 

global-min-publish-age
setting holds back newly published versions by a configurable window, an opt-in defence against malicious crate releases:
[registry]
global-min-publish-age = "3 days"

On Hacker News, developer woodruffw argued cooldowns need to coexist with immediate security patching:

You should do both: you should let normal updates cool down,

and

you should immediately patch security advisories.

One of the biggest ergonomic problems with cooldowns is that many tools let the former goal obstruct the latter. Both should be part of the state machine of resolution itself, rather than things that get layered on.

ImportStatic found on the beta that 

cargo install
ignores the setting entirely and that an update could even downgrade a forced security fix, something the release notes also flag as a known caveat. The approach sits alongside GitHub's Dependabot cooldown protection but builds the age check into dependency resolution itself.

Other notable additions include 

core::mem::DropGuard
for running a closure on every exit path, 
std::mem::conjure_zst
for zero-sized types in unsafe code, plus smaller ergonomic wins such as 
bool::toggle
, 
str::trim_prefix
, 
str::trim_suffix
and 
Box::map
.

Upgrading uses 

rustup update stable
; Rust 1.99 is no longer supported, and 1.101 follows the six-week cadence around 24 December 2026.

Rust is an open-source systems programming language maintained by the Rust Foundation and a global community, designed to empower developers to build reliable and efficient software through strong type safety, memory safety guarantees without a garbage collector, and a mature package ecosystem through Cargo.

entries.title: AWS Lambda Doubles Its Timeout to 30 Minutes After Eight Years at 15
entries.summary: AWS has raised the maximum timeout of on-demand Lambda Event Functions from 15 to 30 minutes in all commercial regions, with no opt-in and no new pricing. The limit had stood since 2018. AWS's post lists the costs: twice the concurrency at the same request rate, three-hour SQS visibility timeouts, and Kafka mappings that must be recreated. Practitioners welcome it and ask what belongs elsewhere. B
entries.content:
AWS recently doubled the maximum timeout of on-demand Lambda Event Functions from 15 to 30 minutes. The new limit applies to synchronous, asynchronous, and event source mapping invocations in all commercial regions, at standard pricing and without an opt-in. The 15-minute ceiling had stood since 2018, after 60 seconds at launch in 2014 and five minutes from 2015.

Raising the limit is a configuration change per function, and Lambda rejects any value above 1,800 seconds with a validation error:

aws lambda update-function-configuration \
    --function-name my-demo-function \
    --timeout 1800

The change covers one of the three shapes Lambda took this year. Web Functions keep 15 minutes, and Lambda MicroVMs allow eight hours, while on Lambda Managed Instances synchronous invocations now get 30 minutes and asynchronous ones keep the 90 minutes introduced in September. AWS names agentic AI requests that chain model and tool calls, media transcoding, Monte Carlo simulations, and report generation as the workloads that outgrew 15 minutes.

According to Tarun Rai Madan, Dan Slusariuc, and Snehil Ameta, the authors of the announcement, the first thing to check before raising the timeout is capacity:

Concurrency equals requests per second multiplied by average duration in seconds. At the same request rate, a function that runs for 30 minutes instead of 15 needs twice the concurrency. For example, 1 request per second at 30 minutes each needs 1,800 concurrent executions.

The rest of the post is about what sits around the function. An SQS queue's visibility timeout has to be at least six times the function timeout, which means three hours. Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams read one batch per shard at a time, so a slow function slows the shard. Amazon MQ, DocumentDB and Kafka mappings created before November 19 stay at 14 minutes. A NAT gateway still drops idle connections after 350 seconds, and the Init phase keeps its 10-second limit.

Wibo van der Sluis, an independent AWS practitioner, tested the SQS rule in eu-west-1 by raising a function to 1,800 seconds behind a queue with a 90-minute visibility timeout and then lowering the queue to 60 seconds. Both changes were accepted with the mapping still enabled, while a new mapping from the same queue was refused:

So the check exists, but only at creation. One more thing the test showed: at creation, Lambda compared the queue with the function timeout itself, not with six times it. I did not test where exactly that line sits, so treat the six times as guidance you enforce yourself.

He adds that an asynchronous function which times out three times has run for 90 minutes before the event reaches a dead-letter queue, and concludes that 30 minutes is the wrong fix for slow code behind an API.

Luc van Donkersgoed, principal engineer at NS and AWS Serverless Hero, writes:

Hell froze over. AWS Lambda now supports 30-minute timeouts. I am not sure how I feel about this.

The comments under the post took two directions. Magnus Eriksson, architect and former AWS employee, notes that Lambda "is anyhow quite expensive per CPU second compared to EC2" and would still reserve it for short-lived spiky loads. Matthew Bonig, AWS DevTools Hero and co-author of The CDK Book, looked further ahead: "Eventually it'll be 8 hours, and then nobody will be able to understand when to use it vs. MicroVMs."

On Reddit, the most-upvoted reply welcomed the change because it avoids Fargate and ECS for hour-long batch jobs. The answer under it was that Fargate is beautifully simple. One commenter sets out where the longer limit fits:

A 30 minute run still bills for the full duration at your configured memory, so check the cost per invocation before moving batch style work here, and keep the handler idempotent with a dead letter queue, because a failure or timeout partway through a long run can leave partial work behind. For multi step work, long running jobs, or anything that needs clear state and retries, Step Functions with Fargate or ECS is still usually cleaner.

Joseph Emison, CTO of Branch Insurance, reads the move as Lambda team recognizing that Cloud Run is its most compelling competitor. Cloud Run services allow 60 minutes per request, and Azure Functions on the Flex Consumption and Premium plans enforce no maximum, with a 60-minute grace period during scale-in. AWS has not said whether the Lambda limit will move again.

entries.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: Automating Spark Upgrades with Codex Agents at OpenAI
entries.summary: At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mouli Mukherjee, Engineering Manager for Data Infrastructure at OpenAI, argued that AI agents are most useful not for rebuilding a data platform, but for the open-ended operational work that is hard to turn into fixed playbooks. By Robert Krzaczyński
entries.content:
At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mouli Mukherjee, Engineering Manager for Data Infrastructure at OpenAI, argued that AI agents are most useful not for rebuilding a data platform, but for the open-ended operational work that is hard to turn into fixed playbooks. OpenAI’s platform runs at exabyte scale, with hundreds of thousands of datasets and a Spark fleet on millions of cores, and Mukherjee showed how Codex-driven agents can take on that kind of work when the right systems sit underneath them.

Mukherjee clearly distinguished between deterministic systems and agents. She stated that anything requiring consistent outputs for the same inputs, such as access control, configuration resolution, and data correctness guarantees, should remain within the realm of proper systems. Agents utilize these systems as tools and do not attempt to reimplement them. As she expressed:

We should definitely build the systems where we want guarantees and guardrails.

Agents earn their place where failure modes and remediations cannot be fully enumerated in advance, such as debugging: follow the evidence, decide what to try next, and stay inside the tools’ guarantees.

The Spark upgrade outlines steps taken to ensure safety. The team first built a shadow-run service for testing, which reused production inputs and operated on a low-priority queue to avoid impacting live operations. They also implemented a configuration override service to prevent experiments from changing global settings and developed a validation skill to compare production and shadow runs. After these safeguards were in place, agents claimed jobs, launched shadow runs, reviewed validation reports, classified errors, and transitioned jobs to the new Spark version.

Mukherjee reported that the same primitives now cover more of routine platform operations. Agents can tune job efficiency continuously by inspecting query plans, trying a config change, comparing runs, and iterating. For lower-risk incremental library releases, the team sometimes skips the shadow step and promotes directly, trading capacity for higher rollback risk. Jobs that pass shadow validation but later fail in production can auto-roll back to the previous Spark version so pipelines keep running without manual intervention. On the support side, agents can search past incident reports, suggest runbook updates, trace why a table is stale through orchestrator and scheduler logs, and help users understand access-control denials, while permissions still enforce the user’s own credentials.

Mukherjee recommended starting with the repetitive, open-ended tasks where judgment matters and failure modes are too numerous to hard-code, building the safety mechanisms first, and only then letting agents operate inside those bounds so experimentation stays repeatable, observable, and reversible.

entries.title: CNCF Research Shows Virtual Machines Remain Central as AI Workloads Evolve
entries.summary: New research from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and Linux Foundation Research finds that VMs host an average of 53% of production applications, while emerging AI and agentic workloads are creating additional demand for virtualisation, particularly where stronger execution isolation is required. By Craig Risi
entries.content:
Virtual machines (VMs) continue to account for a substantial share of cloud-native production infrastructure, despite the widespread adoption of containers and Kubernetes. New research from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and Linux Foundation Research finds that VMs host an average of 53% of production applications, while emerging AI and agentic workloads are creating additional demand for virtualisation, particularly where stronger execution isolation is required.

The report surveyed 492 cloud-native practitioners and technology leaders in September 2026. Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 34% identified AI and agentic workloads as a contributing factor. The findings suggest that rather than replacing virtual machines with containers, organisations are increasingly combining the two to accommodate different application and security requirements.

The research challenges the assumption that cloud-native adoption necessarily means moving away from virtual machines. While containers provide portability and efficient application packaging, VMs continue to offer isolation and support for workloads that depend on dedicated operating systems or established virtualisation environments.

The survey found that 51% of respondents run at least half of their production applications on VMs. This rises to an average of 64% in organisations with more than 10,000 employees, compared with 45% among organisations with fewer than 500 employees.

Furthermore, 71% of respondents who provided both current and expected workload figures anticipate their VM share remaining within the same range over the next year. This points towards continued coexistence rather than a wholesale migration to one deployment model.

One of the more significant findings concerns the relationship between AI adoption and infrastructure security.

AI agents increasingly generate and execute code, interact with tools, and access external systems. This creates new risks when generated code is executed in environments containing sensitive data or shared infrastructure.

Virtual machines offer a stronger isolation boundary than conventional containers, which share the host operating system kernel. The report identifies hardware-level VM isolation, containers running inside VMs, and MicroVM sandboxing as approaches organisations are using to contain AI workloads.

Among organisations expanding their VM footprint, 47% cited security and isolation as a contributing factor, while 34% specifically identified AI and agentic workloads.

The survey also points to growing interest in stronger isolation technologies. MicroVM sandboxing adoption is expected to increase from 20% current use to 30% planned use, while confidential computing is expected to grow from 12% to 26%. These figures represent reported intentions rather than confirmed deployments.

Some 61% of respondents described their VM and container administration teams as collaborative or fully integrated, suggesting that managing different workload types is increasingly becoming a shared platform engineering responsibility.

Kubernetes is also beginning to play a role in virtual machine management. Among respondents using VMs, 8% reported using KubeVirt, the CNCF project that allows virtual machines to be managed through Kubernetes resources and APIs.

This brings VM lifecycle management into existing Kubernetes operational practices without requiring applications to abandon their virtualised environments.

The findings reinforce a shift in how cloud-native infrastructure is evolving. Kubernetes and containers remain important, but they are not necessarily the right execution model for every workload.

Technologies such as KubeVirt and Kata Containers show how virtualisation can integrate with container orchestration, while MicroVMs provide lightweight environments to isolate short-lived or potentially untrusted workloads.

For platform engineering teams, the research highlights the need to accommodate different execution environments without fragmenting operational practices. AI adds another dimension, making isolation, resource utilisation and workload security increasingly important infrastructure considerations.

The survey was sponsored by CNCF and Broadcom, and its results should be read as reported industry perspectives rather than a complete census of cloud-native deployments. Nevertheless, its findings provide a useful indication of where infrastructure priorities are moving.

entries.title: OpenAI Scales Git for Coding Agents with Pando
entries.summary: OpenAI has detailed Pando, a new backend that scales Git for concurrent coding-agent workloads without replacing familiar Git workflows. The company reports nearly 80% lower median push latency by coordinating branch updates independently and reusing stored packfiles across fetches. By Eran Stiller
entries.content:
OpenAI has detailed Pando, a new backend that scales Git for concurrent coding-agent workloads without replacing familiar Git workflows. The company reports nearly 80% lower median push latency by coordinating branch updates independently and reusing stored packfiles across fetches.

Pando now powers all development in OpenAI's monorepo and is serving nearly a petabyte of Git data per day. OpenAI attributes the increased load to Codex-driven development, and each push can in turn trigger multiple CI jobs that all fetch the same history. Pando went into production in April 2026.

Rather than replace Git's client and protocol, OpenAI has changed how the backend coordinates reference updates and stores and transfers objects. On a push, Pando validates the incoming packfile as it's being streamed to immutable blob storage, without unpacking it into a local repository. A metadata transaction records the reference version (containing the new branch tip, the packfile and its dependencies on earlier reference versions) and atomically updates the reference pointer. Updates to unrelated references can proceed independently of one another; updates to the same reference still need to be coordinated.

OpenAI refers to this as causal consistency with serialisable updates to individual references and read-your-own-write consistency. A reader gets the history needed for the requested revision, but fetching a number of branches won't provide a repository-wide snapshot. Two clients can see different combinations of branch versions during concurrent updates. The trade-off removes a shared coordination point for unrelated pushes.

Pando also changes how Git decides which objects to transfer. By default, when a client pushes a new feature branch, the server will advertise only a designated trunk branch as its base. That constrains the dependencies of the resulting packfile, which in turn allows Pando to reuse it for readers who already have that trunk history. Repeated or stacked branch pushes can resend objects outside trunk, trading some additional bandwidth for the benefit of reusable packs.



Pando’s topic-branch packs depend on advertised trunk history and can repeat objects from earlier pushes (source)

For fetches, Pando maps the client's existing and requested commits to reference versions and picks out the appropriate stored packs to cover the missing history. Git's packfile-uri capability allows the server to return download links rather than generate a bespoke pack for each client. Express, a regional pack-delivery cache, serves those downloads. OpenAI reports cache-hit rates in excess of 99% and tests in which clone and fetch operations saturated 10 Gbps network links.

Background compaction groups packs into larger, geometrically sized covers, resembling compaction in a log-structured merge-tree. The covers provide better compression and act as a skip-list-like index for fetch planning. Pando keeps packs at every level so that clients with different histories can still be served.



Pando groups successive packs into larger covers to improve compression and fetch planning, retaining packs at every level (source)

The design contrasts with Anthropic's Scion, previously covered by InfoQ. Scion replaces Git's underlying model with changesets recording files changed relative to their first parent and content-addressed pointers to compressed file contents; commits, merges, rebases and history queries run server-side. Its clients retrieve missing immutable trees and blobs, rather than negotiate Git packfiles, and use bounded local caches and sparse or virtualised checkouts.

Both systems make use of immutable data and regional caches to reduce repeated computation. The way in which they draw the compatibility line is very different, though. Pando preserves Git's object model and client-side workflows and changes the backend coordination and delivery. Scion, on the other hand, assumes an online client and moves the repository operations into a dedicated service. The improvements they report are not directly comparable. OpenAI reports on push latency, whereas Anthropic reports on checkout speedups and infrastructure reductions compared with its previous Git-based setup.

Git compatibility did not eliminate migration work. OpenAI initially deployed Pando as a read- and write-through proxy, moved clients in phases, and migrated hundreds of integrations using legacy APIs, webhooks and repository downloads. It also distributed its own Git build, which supports parallel downloading and indexing of independent packs. OpenAI says some client improvements are already upstream, with others available in its public repository.

For the architects, it's a case of two separate decisions: which source control operations go on the server and which of the consistency and transfer guarantees do the workloads actually need. Pando retains the Git workflows but dispenses with the repository-wide snapshot across branches and accepts redundant transfers in order to reduce the amount of coordination and per-fetch computation.

entries.title: Presentation: Inferencing for Enterprises
entries.summary: Dio Rettori discusses the operational realities of enterprise AI inference. Moving beyond fast token generation, he explores why inference requires dedicated systems engineering, tackles GPU utilization pitfalls, compares on-prem versus cloud TCO, and analyzes multi-agent latency determinism. He shares why teams must embed domain ontology directly into models rather than relying solely on RAG. By
